system:
You are a computational scientist who builds mechanistic models of biochemical and pharmacological processes from experimental data. You have no model library: write every candidate model yourself as custom code for fit_model. Work the way a careful scientist does:

1. Plan: call write_plan first with a short list of steps; update it if your approach changes.
2. Look before you fit: inspect the data and use run_python for quick numeric checks that discriminate mechanisms.
3. Hypothesise: record at least two competing hypotheses with record_hypothesis, each with what it predicts in these data. Update their status as evidence comes in.
4. Test: fit competing models with the same error model and compare BIC, residual diagnostics and identifiability. Fit independent models in the same turn to save steps.
5. Revise: if a model leaves structured residuals, work out what the data do that it does not allow, and write a better model.
6. Stay honest: always consider the simplest model, including no effect at all. Report parameters the data cannot determine. Never state a number that did not come from a tool result.
7. Submit with submit_model (mechanism_label 'custom'), citing fit_ids as evidence.

You have at most 20 model turns, so be efficient.
task_prompt:
Initial reaction rates v (uM/min) of a purified enzyme were measured at substrate concentrations S (uM) and inhibitor concentrations I (uM). Each condition was measured in duplicate; rates carry additive measurement noise.

The data table has 80 rows with columns: S, I, v. Your model will be used to predict rates at much higher inhibitor concentrations.

Find the mechanistic model that best explains these data, fit it, check it critically, and submit it.

content.thinking:
Every MM-type model fails the runs test, so the structure is strong. Even the I=0 group fits poorly. Its data looks sigmoidal: v climbs steeply at low S, going from 0.48 at S=0.25 to 1.84 at S=0.5.

I'm weighing whether a Hill-type curve with n>1, a lag, or substrate activation could explain the steep rise at low S, and I'm planning to fit Hill-type models with and without inhibition. First I'll print the full dataset.

I'm comparing the apparent Vmax at I=20 against I=0, where the ratio comes out around 0.4, and I=8 looks similar. Inhibition seems to saturate at high inhibitor concentrations, which points toward partial inhibition, and I'm working out what that implies for the mechanism.

I'm checking whether the noise at I=0 is proportional rather than constant, since the low-S spread there is much wider than at I=20. The model also misses in a patterned way, underpredicting at I=0 and overpredicting at higher inhibitor levels, so I'm weighing whether the inhibition isn't simply mixed. I'll test a few alternatives: a Hill coefficient on substrate, one on inhibitor, and a model with a nonzero floor.

I'm now writing out the partial-inhibition form of the rate law, where the fraction left uninhibited is set by the inhibitor term, and I'm noting that this is essentially the general mixed model in another guise. I'm also considering that the general mixed form already captures a maximal inhibition level set by the ratio of the two inhibition constants, so the extra parameter may be redundant. I'll next try a Hill coefficient on substrate and see whether it helps.

I'm going to try a two-site model alongside the Hill-type variants, fitting a mixed model with a Hill coefficient on substrate, another with one on inhibitor, and a competitive model with an inhibitor-dependent Vmax floor. I'll also refit using a proportional error model to see whether the noise pattern changes the picture.

content.thinking:
The fit with the inhibitor Hill term at h=0.32 improves BIC a lot, from -16 to -196.8. An exponent that low means the inhibitor effect is sub-linear and probably saturates, something like a log or a saturating form. The residuals still show structure (runs z=-3.3), and this fit used additive error with sigma 0.26.

I'm weighing whether inhibitor binding might work through two sites, a high-affinity one and a low-affinity one, instead of a single Hill term. The steep early drop at low inhibitor concentration and the flatter response after that could fit that picture. I'm also checking whether tight-binding kinetics would produce a sharper transition than the sub-linear behaviour I'm seeing, which seems to argue against it.

I'm going to try three variants: a noncompetitive Hill form with a floor, a two-population partial inhibition model with separate affinities, and a mixed model with two inhibitor sites, each keeping the Hill exponent.

I'm wrapping up the thought about the log-type dependence and deciding to just run the candidate models and compare them.

content.thinking:
I'm noting that the fit10 model was a poor fit due to a bug in my code, so I'm setting it aside. Fit8 and fit9 look solid, with fit8 being a two-population partial inhibition model that reduces effectively to about four parameters, since K2 isn't identifiable. I'm now working out how much of the population is uninhibited under fit8.

I'm settling on fit8 with K2 taken to infinity, which gives a simpler four-parameter model where a fraction of the enzyme is inhibited and the rest isn't. I'll fit that version with the Hill coefficient fixed at 1, since fit9's Hill value near 0.9 suggests that's enough. A quick check at high inhibitor concentration gives an asymptote near 4 at high substrate, which is close to the observed value of about 3.8 at I=20, S=32, so it looks consistent.

content.thinking:
I'm looking at fit 11, which has the best BIC at -243.9 with four parameters, all identified and no extra structure. Its mechanism looks like noncompetitive inhibition with Km unchanged, but only partial: about 40% of enzyme activity ignores the inhibitor, and the rest is inhibited with Ki of 0.51 µM. That is not the standard full noncompetitive model, where Ki equals Ka and inhibition is complete.

I'm weighing whether the pure noncompetitive model, with c=0, is already in the earlier fits. Fit 4 was a mixed model, so probably not. Fit 11 is far better by BIC, -243.9 against -16, so I'm fairly confident in it and will record the hypotheses and move on without more fitting.
